before.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark “Explain Two with Sources,” cite either Hebrews 1:1–4 (revelation through Jesus) or Genesis 15 (Abraham covenant vision) or John 4:43–54 (the royal official’s son). A paraphrase without the reference earns only 4 marks at most. For the 12-mark Discuss question, remember to develop the Hume/Dawkins counter-argument in full — examiners note that students often write only one sentence on the opposing view. For divergent Christian views on visions, contrast Catholic (formal approval process, Magisterium) with Protestant (scripture as the primary test). SPaG marks reward correct spelling of: covenant, revelation, Transfiguration, Hume.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: God has revealed himself through the prophets and scriptures (1); the covenants with Noah and Abraham are key moments of revelation showing God's faithfulness and personal concern (1); Jesus Christ is the fullest and final revelation of God — Hebrews 1:1-4 (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe happened at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a mountain (1); his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light; Moses and Elijah appeared with him (1); God's voice declared from a cloud 'This is my Son whom I love — listen to him' (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe the covenants with Noah and Abraham provide evidence for God's existence.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The covenant with Noah shows God's care and faithfulness to all creation — God promises never to destroy all life by flood again, revealing a personal God who acts in history (2); the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) is a visionary encounter in which God promises descendants as numerous as the stars, showing God initiates personal relationships and makes binding promises (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe miracles provide evidence for the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The healing in John 4:43-54 — where the official's son recovered at the exact moment Jesus spoke — suggests God has power over natural processes, supporting belief in an omnipotent creator (2); miracles produce faith in those who witness them, suggesting they originate from a divine source rather than natural coincidence (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles and visions prove that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: miracles (John 4:43-54) and visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17:1-13) show God communicating directly; transformed lives and unexplained healings support this. Counter: Hume's argument that natural law always makes doubt more rational than acceptance; Dawkins on visions as brain chemistry; only anecdote supports miracles. Evaluate which position is stronger with reasoning. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, covenant, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about visions, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catholic Christianity formally evaluates reported visions through the Church's Magisterium — only approved visions are accepted as reliable, with Hebrews 1:1-4 confirming that any vision must align with Christ as the fullness of revelation (2); many Protestant Christians hold that scripture (sola scriptura) is the sole reliable source of revelation, so personal visions should always be tested against biblical teaching — the Transfiguration (Matthew 17) is paradigmatic but personal visions today are secondary to scripture (2); source credit for Hebrews 1:1-4 or Matthew 17:1-13 explicitly named (1).

lessons.title: Religious Experience, Prayer, Design and Cosmological Arguments

before.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers four arguments in one — make sure you can write specifically about each one rather than blurring them together. The most dangerous error is confusing Aquinas’s Three Ways (a posteriori, from observation) with the Ontological Argument (a priori, from concept alone) — the latter is not on this course. For the 5-mark source question, Romans 1:18–24 is the named biblical anchor for the design argument: cite book, chapter and verse. For prayer as evidence, cite 1 John 5:13–17. For religious experience, Exodus 3 (burning bush). For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Dawkins/Humanist counter-argument fully — one sentence is not enough. SPaG marks: cosmological, contingency, teleological, Aquinas.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: everything in motion was moved by something else — there must be an unmoved first mover (1); every effect has a cause — there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things might not exist — there must be a necessary being (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the experience of Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3) is used as evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Moses encountered a bush that burned without being consumed (1); God spoke to Moses from the fire, calling him by name and revealing his identity (1); the experience transformed Moses and led him to a life-changing mission, suggesting it originated from a real divine source (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe answered prayer is evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Many Christians report specific outcomes that followed prayer — healing, guidance, provision — which they cannot explain except by God's action (2); 1 John 5:13-17 teaches that God hears those who ask according to his will, suggesting prayer involves real communication with a present and responsive God (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for believing the design argument supports the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The fine-tuning of the universe — physical constants are set so precisely that life would be impossible if they varied slightly — suggests intentional design by a creator (2); Romans 1:18-24 states that God's 'eternal power and divine nature' are 'clearly seen' in what has been made, providing scriptural support for the design argument (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 named explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious experience is the most convincing evidence that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Exodus 3 (Moses), answered prayer (1 John 5:13-17), and the transforming effect of religious experience suggest genuine divine encounter. Counter: Dawkins argues experiences are brain-generated; Hume argues subjectivity means experiences provide no objective proof. Evaluate whether personal experience is stronger or weaker than philosophical arguments (design, cosmological). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: religious experience, cosmological, revelation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which atheist and Humanist arguments challenge the design argument, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per challenge; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows biological complexity arises through natural selection without requiring a designer — Dawkins calls this a 'blind watchmaker' (2); the existence of suffering and 'bad design' (vestigial organs, disease, extinction) suggests that if the universe was designed, the designer is not all-loving and all-powerful (2); source credit for Romans 1:18-24 used in counter-framing, or Darwin cited explicitly (1).

before.exam_tip_html: This is a short spec point (3B 1.8) but it generates rich discussion questions. For the 5-mark source answer, Proverbs 22:6 is the named anchor — use the book, chapter and verse. For the 12-mark Discuss, present Dawkins’s indoctrination argument fully (not just in one sentence) and give the Christian responses in equal depth. A common error is to treat religious upbringing as a weak argument and spend most of the 12 marks attacking it — remember to argue both sides with equal development. For the 3-mark Outline question, give three discrete features of Christian upbringing (e.g. baptism, Sunday school, prayer at home) as separate bullet-style points, not one extended answer. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of a Christian upbringing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete features: infant baptism or dedication (1); regular church attendance and involvement in the church community (1); prayer at home, including bedtime prayers and saying grace (1). Other valid features include Sunday school, faith schools, Christian festivals. Three distinct points required.

practice_questions.text: Describe Richard Dawkins's argument that religious upbringing is a form of indoctrination.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Dawkins argues there is no such thing as a 'Christian child' — only a child of Christian parents (1); he argues that labelling children with their parents' religion and teaching it before the child can evaluate it critically is a form of intellectual coercion (1); he claims in The God Delusion (2006) that this amounts to a form of harm to the child (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe religious upbringing may lead to genuine belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Regular worship and prayer creates deep emotional and spiritual pathways from childhood that anchor faith through adult challenges, suggesting the belief is genuinely held rather than merely inherited (2); the fact that many adults who were raised as Christians continue in faith after having the opportunity to leave suggests the upbringing transmitted something real about God rather than just cultural habit (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian reasons for raising children in the faith, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Proverbs 22:6 ('Start children off on the way they should go, and even when they are old they will not turn from it') teaches that early formation shapes lifelong character and faith — parents are commanded to provide this foundation (2); Christian community gives the child role models of lived faith, showing that belief is practised by real, trustworthy adults — this embodied witness is more powerful than abstract argument for a young person (2); source credit for Proverbs 22:6 named with chapter and verse (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Religious upbringing is the most important reason why people believe in God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: Proverbs 22:6 supports the practice; upbringing creates genuine, lasting faith; millions of adults with a Christian upbringing freely choose to continue in faith. Counter: Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006) argues it is indoctrination before critical evaluation; many leave the faith; upbringing-based belief doesn't prove God exists — it only explains why people believe. Evaluate: is upbringing-based belief less 'genuine' than belief reached through argument? Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: indoctrination, upbringing, Proverbs.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue religious upbringing may lead to a rejection of belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: If a child later encounters intellectual challenges to faith (such as the problem of evil) that their upbringing never addressed, they may conclude the beliefs were given without adequate reason and abandon them (2); Dawkins argues in The God Delusion (2006) that children raised in a faith before they can evaluate it critically have been denied the opportunity to reach their own informed conclusions, and some will eventually exercise that right by leaving (2); source credit for Proverbs 22:6 in counter-argument framing, or Dawkins The God Delusion cited explicitly (1).
